common.title: District River Management Plan
common.heading: 1. ABOUT THE DISTRICT RIVER MANAGEMENT PLAN

subsections.heading: 1.1 The Narmada
paragraphs: The Narmada is the largest river of Madhya Pradesh and, at 1,312 km, one of the longest rivers in India. It rises on the Amarkantak plateau in Anuppur district, flows west through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, and enters the Gulf of Khambhat about 30 km west of Bharuch. About 30 major dams, including Indira Sagar, Sardar Sarovar, Omkareshwar, Bargi and Tawa, regulate its flow. The towns along its banks draw drinking water from the river and, where sewerage is incomplete, return untreated wastewater to it through natural drains.

subsections.heading: 1.2 What the DRMP is
paragraphs: The District River Management Plan (DRMP) is a city-level planning framework, that supports Nirmal Dhara through integrated urban water management. Rather than treating wastewater on its own, the DRMP aims to close the urban water cycle: water supply, sewage generation, collection and treatment, drains and their outfalls into the river, flood risk, and reuse of treated water.

subsections.heading: 1.3 Scope of this report
paragraphs: The Urban Development and Housing Department (UDHD), Government of Madhya Pradesh, is implementing sewerage projects in 21 towns on the banks of the Narmada. They are funded by the Asian Development Bank (5 towns), the World Bank (4), a state special fund (6), KfW of Germany (5), and AMRUT in Jabalpur. Sewerage in Amarkantak, Bhedaghat, Budni and Dharampuri is complete, and treated water there is reused for gardening, brick kilns, road washing, curing of construction and vehicle washing. The DRMP covers these 21 urban local bodies (ULBs), from Amarkantak downstream to Barwani and Sendhwa.

subsections.heading: 1.4 How each city chapter is organised
bullets: City profile, existing water supply and sewerage, and the ULB’s own future plans.

STP analysis: ward-wise population and sewage projected to 2050 at 108 litres per person per day (135 lpcd supply, 80% return); GIS-based multi-criteria site suitability (elevation 40%, flood risk 20%, and proximity to sewers, streams and drains and wind direction, 10% each); K-Means service zones; proposed decentralised STPs, their capacities and adjacent water bodies.
Key findings and recommendations for each city.

cities.name: Amarkantak
cities.subtitle: Amarkantak Nagar Parishad · Anuppur district
cities.intro: Amarkantak, where the Narmada rises, is a Nagar Parishad of 15 wards in Anuppur district, about 550 km from Bhopal, with 8,416 residents. Its sewerage system (1.20 MLD STP, 32 km of sewers) is complete, and a 2.09 MLD water supply scheme drawing on the Narmada is under construction.

future_plans: Upgrading and building ghats
Public amenities

cities.name: Jabalpur
cities.subtitle: Jabalpur Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation) · Jabalpur district
cities.intro: Jabalpur, the largest city on the Narmada, is a Municipal Corporation of 79 wards (36,700 ha) with about 14.98 lakh residents, 320 km from Bhopal. Under JNNURM and AMRUT, 13 of 15 sanctioned STPs (154.38 of 160.38 MLD) and 465.56 of 472.93 km of sewers are built, but only 35,000 houses are connected to the sewers against 1,03,942 sanctioned connections.
future_plans: Upgrading and building ghats, community halls and public amenities

The population year is not stated; 14.98 lakh is well above the Census 2011 count, so it is likely a current estimate.
